title: Jira from code

story: Every minute, the Jira poll asks Jira one question: which RH tickets are assigned to Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent? This morning the answer includes RH-1234. Before a run can start, the poll needs one more fact: the requester, the person who handed the ticket to Nova. The requester is the only person who may approve Nova's plan, and the one person who may never approve Nova's PR, so getting the name wrong breaks a safety rule.

RH-1234 has a messy history. Omer, a teammate, wrote it last month. A week ago Dana, another teammate, assigned it to Nova by mistake and took it back one minute later. This morning Sean assigned it to Nova for real. The reporter field says Omer, the first hand-over says Dana, and the latest one says Sean.
hook.question: How does code find Nova's tickets in Jira, and how does it know for sure who handed each one over?

p: The poll needs two facts from Jira, and it gets each one from a different place. Which tickets are Nova's comes from a search. Who handed each ticket over comes from the ticket's changelog, the list Jira keeps of every change to an issue. Both are plain HTTPS calls to Jira's REST API (version 3) with JSON in and out, the same shape of API you already know from GitHub.

The poll calls Jira as Nova. Nova is a Jira user of its own, a service account, which means an account that belongs to a program instead of a person. Jira names every user by an accountId, a long string like 712020:4c1d0e…, and uses it everywhere: in the assignee field, as a comment's author, and in the changelog. GET /rest/api/3/myself returns the caller's own accountId, so the poll asks once who it is and remembers the answer.

JQL, the Jira Query Language, is the filter text you can type into Jira's search box, and the API accepts the same text. Nova's query asks for RH tickets assigned to the caller that are not done yet, oldest change first. Because the poll runs as Nova, currentUser() means Nova. Sorting by updated ASC makes the ticket that has waited longest come first.

The search endpoint is POST /rest/api/3/search/jql. It answers in pages. When there are more results than fit in one page, the answer includes a nextPageToken, and you send the same request again with that token to get the next page. This is a cursor: a bookmark that the server gives you, instead of a page number you compute yourself. Stop only when an answer has no token. A poll that reads only the first page does not fail with an error; it quietly never sees the tickets on page two.

notes.text: Runs as the Nova service account, so currentUser() is Nova.
Ask only for the fields the poll needs. Never attachments: they can hold customer data.
On the first call nextPageToken is undefined, so JSON.stringify leaves it out.
No token in the answer means this was the last page.

read.h: Who handed it over: the changelog
p: Back to the messy history of RH-1234. The reporter is the person who wrote the ticket, and that is not the same as the person who asked Nova to do it. Comments prove nothing either, because anyone can write one. The changelog is different: Jira writes it itself, every time a field changes, with the author and the time. Nobody can edit it.

GET /rest/api/3/issue/RH-1234/changelog returns the changes oldest first. Each entry has an author and a list of items, one per changed field, with from and to. For the assignee field, from and to are accountIds. So the rule is: keep the entries that set the assignee to Nova, and take the author of the last one. For RH-1234 that skips Dana's mistake from last week and names Sean. If no entry matches, there is no requester, and no run starts.

notes.text: The Slack path, explained just below: our app wrote the requester onto the ticket.
jira.me is Nova's own accountId, read once from /myself.
at(-1) is the last match: the most recent hand-over wins. at(0) would name Dana.

read.see:
who: Dana  2026-10-05T09:00  assignee -> 712020:nova
who: Dana  2026-10-05T09:01  assignee -> null
who: Omer  2026-10-07T14:00  status -> 3
who: Sean  2026-10-13T08:58  assignee -> 712020:nova      <- the requester

deeper.h: Go deeper: the Slack path and issue properties
p: People can also hand a ticket over by typing /nova RH-1234 in Slack. Then our Slack app, not a person, changes the assignee, so the changelog would name Nova itself. To keep the person's name, the app first stores it on the ticket as an issue property: a small JSON value that an app keeps on an issue under a key, here nova.requester. People do not see properties in Jira's screens, and setting one notifies nobody.

The calls are PUT and GET /rest/api/3/issue/RH-1234/properties/nova.requester. When the property was never set, the GET answers 404, which here is an answer and not an error, so the client turns it into undefined. That is why requesterOf looks at the property first and only then reads the changelog.

A poll calls Jira every minute, forever, so it must be polite and safe to repeat. Polite means it respects Jira's rate limits. When Jira gets too many requests it answers 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header that says how many seconds to wait. The client waits exactly that long and tries again. Retrying at once only makes the limit last longer.

Safe to repeat means the poll can see RH-1234 sixty times in an hour without doing anything sixty times. That comes from the lesson on run names: the poll starts the run through startRun with the ID nova:RH-1234, so every later sighting joins the open run. And the poll must never react to its own actions. When Nova assigns the ticket back to Sean or edits its status comment, those changes are Nova's, and the code skips them by checking the author against Nova's accountId.

notes.text: One function adds the auth header for every Jira call, so no caller can forget it.
Retry-After is in seconds. Wait exactly that long.
For lookups like an issue property, 404 means "not set".
Anything else that fails throws. The Temporal activity around the poll retries it later.

lab.title: Find the requester in a pretend Jira
lab.goal: Run one poll against a local Jira with recorded answers: read every page of a JQL search, survive a 429, and name the right requester from the changelog.

guess.q: RH-1234's changelog says: Dana assigned it to Nova, Dana unassigned it a minute later, and a week later Sean assigned it to Nova. Omer is the reporter. Who should the poll name as the requester?

options.text: Omer, because he wrote the ticket.
options.why: Writing a ticket is not handing it to Nova. The reporter is never read for this.

options.text: Dana, because she handed it to Nova first.
options.why: Her hand-over was undone a minute later. Taking the first match is a real bug, and the Fix it step shows what it causes.

options.text: Sean, because his is the latest change that set the assignee to Nova.
options.why: The last matching changelog entry wins, so the person who handed it over most recently owns the run.

follow.say: Make a folder, then create the pretend Jira. It answers the few endpoints the poll uses with recorded data, and it rate-limits the first search on purpose.
Start it in the first terminal and leave it open. It prints every request it receives.
In the second terminal, ask who you are. The poll does this once, because it needs Nova's own accountId to read the changelog.
Search the way the poll does. The first search is rate-limited, so look at the status line and the Retry-After header.
follow.do: curl -si -X POST localhost:4000/rest/api/3/search/jql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"jql":"assignee = currentUser()"}' | head -3
follow.see:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
content-type: application/json
Retry-After: 2

follow.say: Wait two seconds and search again. This time you get the first page and a token for the next one.
follow.do: curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/rest/api/3/search/jql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"jql":"assignee = currentUser()"}' | jq -c '{keys: [.issues[].key], nextPageToken}'

follow.say: Read RH-1234's changelog, one line per change, and find the requester yourself before the code does.

Now the poll itself: one fetch function that waits on 429, a search that reads every page, and requesterOf. Stop the fake Jira with Ctrl+C and start it again first, so the poll meets the rate limit too.
follow.see:
Jira said 429, waiting 2 s
start nova:RH-1234 for Sean
start nova:RH-1239 for Omer
skip  RH-1241: no requester found

lab.build: RH-1241 was handed over in Slack, so its only assignee change was made by Nova itself, and the poll skips it. Our Slack app stored the person as the issue property nova.requester. Look at it with curl -s localhost:4000/rest/api/3/issue/RH-1241/properties/nova.requester, then change requesterOf so it reads that property first (jiraFetch gives back undefined on a 404) and falls back to the changelog. Run node poll.mjs again.
checks: node poll.mjs prints three lines, one for each of RH-1234, RH-1239 and RH-1241, so the second page was read.
RH-1234 starts for Sean, not for Dana or Omer.
RH-1241 starts for 712020:omer, the accountId from the issue property.
The fake Jira's terminal shows the search being sent again after the 429, and not sooner than two seconds later.
Running node poll.mjs twice prints the same lines both times: the poll is safe to repeat.
lab.fix: Someone changed toNova.at(-1) to toNova.at(0) "to respect who asked first". Make that change and run node poll.mjs: RH-1234 now starts for Dana, who gave the ticket back a week ago. In the real platform she would be asked to approve Sean's plan, and Sean, the person who really asked, could approve the PR alone. Put at(-1) back and explain in one sentence why the last hand-over must win.
explain: Why does the poll read the changelog instead of the ticket's reporter field?
What happens to a ticket on page two if the search reads only one page, and why would nobody notice?
The poll sees RH-1234 every minute. What makes the sixtieth sighting do nothing?
lab.done: node poll.mjs starts all three tickets with the right requester, and you stopped the fake Jira with Ctrl+C.

check.q: A search answers with 100 issues and a nextPageToken. What should the poll do?

options.text: Stop: one page is enough for a poll that runs every minute
options.why: The tickets on later pages would never start a run, and no error would ever say so.

options.text: Send the same search again with that nextPageToken, and repeat until an answer has no token
options.why: The token is a cursor from the server. No token means the last page.

options.text: Send the same search again with startAt: 100
options.why: This endpoint pages with a token, not with an offset you compute yourself.

check.q: Why does the poll take the requester from the changelog instead of from the newest comment that says "@Nova please do this"?

options.text: Anyone can write a comment, but only Jira writes the changelog, and assigning a ticket needs a permission
options.why: The changelog is Jira's own record of who changed the assignee. A comment is text anyone could type, including text pasted from somewhere else.

options.text: Comments cannot be read through the API
options.why: They can. The problem is that a comment proves nothing about who handed the ticket over.

options.text: The changelog is faster to read
options.why: Speed is not the reason. Trust is.

check.q: Jira answers a search with 429 and Retry-After: 30. What is right?

options.text: Retry at once, up to five times, to get the data quickly
options.why: Hammering a rate-limited API makes the limit last longer for everyone, us included.

options.text: Fail the poll; it runs again in a minute anyway
options.why: A failed activity is retried too, but without waiting it would just hit the limit again. Waiting the time Jira asks for is the fix.

options.text: Wait 30 seconds, then send the same request again
options.why: Jira tells you exactly how long to wait. The client honours it and tries again.

p: The Jira client lives in shared/src/jira.ts in the ai-agents repo and uses Node's own fetch with Jira REST v3; it pages every search, reads changelogs and comments, and honours Retry-After. Nova's poll is one entry in the orchestrator's registry of Jira queries, which ensureSchedules turns into the Temporal schedule poll-jira-nova: every minute, overlap SKIP. Each match goes through startRun, so nova:RH-1234 is started once and joined after that.

The poll runs as the Nova service account with a scoped API token from Vault (infrastructure/ai-agents/jira-nova), synced only to the orchestrator workers. A VM never holds a Jira token: inside a run, Jira calls go through the broker's one-issue scope. The same client keeps one Nova status comment per ticket, edited with notifyUsers=false, and sets the Nova state field.

tickets.why: The Jira client (search with pages, changelog, rate limits) and the registry of Jira queries run by schedules.
The Nova service account, NOVA_JQL and requesterOf: the property first, then the latest assignee change to Nova.
/nova in Slack sets nova.requester and assigns the ticket; the poll reads @Nova commands in new comments.
One status comment edited in place and the Nova state field, through the same client.

words.plain: Jira Query Language: the filter text that finds issues, typed in the search box or sent to the API.
Jira's ID for a user, used for the assignee, comment authors and the changelog.
The cursor a search returns when more results exist; send it back to get the next page.
Jira's own list of every change to an issue, with the author and the time, oldest first.
The header on a 429 answer that says how many seconds to wait before trying again.
A small hidden JSON value an app stores on an issue under a key, like nova.requester.

review.q: From memory: the JQL Nova's poll runs, and why currentUser() means Nova.
review.a: project = RH AND assignee = currentUser() AND statusCategory != Done ORDER BY updated ASC. The poll calls Jira as the Nova service account, so the current user is Nova.

review.q: Explain requesterOf in two sentences to a teammate.
review.a: First it reads the nova.requester property, which our Slack app sets when someone hands over with /nova. Otherwise it reads the changelog and takes the author of the latest change that set the assignee to Nova; no such change means no run.

review.q: Name two ways a poll can hurt Jira or itself, and the fix for each.
review.a: Ignoring 429 (fix: wait for Retry-After); reacting to its own changes, like Nova's assign-back (fix: skip changes whose author is Nova). Also: reading only the first page (fix: loop until no nextPageToken).

remember: Search with JQL to the last page, and take the requester from the changelog's latest hand-over to Nova, never from what someone wrote.
